title: Chinese almond cookies
subtitle: crisp, sandy almond biscuits with a whole almond pressed in the centre
excerpt: Chinese almond cookies are a crisp, slightly sandy biscuit with a pronounced almond flavour, each topped with a single whole almond pressed into the centre before baking. They are a staple of Chinese-American bakeries and are made for Lunar New Year. The texture is closer to a crumbly shortbread than a chewy cookie, and the combination of almond flour and all-purpose flour gives them a more refined flavour than a biscuit made with almond extract alone.
sourceNotes: Chinese almond cookies (杏仁饼, xìng rén bǐng) are associated with Chinese-American bakeries and have roots in traditional Chinese walnut and almond pastries. The version popular in the West developed in the early 20th century as part of the Chinese-American cooking tradition. They are commonly made for Lunar New Year celebrations, as the round shape symbolises coins and the almond topping completeness. The method is documented in Chinese-American cookery books from the mid-20th century onward.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked and cooled cookies in an airtight container for up to 1 month.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keep in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 1 week. They crisp further over 24 hours.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: conventional; 14 to 16 minutes until pale golden at the edges

items.prepNote: 1 for the dough, 1 beaten for egg wash

content.text: Chinese almond cookies have a crumbly, sandy texture that comes from cold butter rubbed into a mixture of plain flour and almond flour. The dough comes together like a shortbread and is shaped by hand into small rounds rather than rolled. Press the whole almond into each round before baking; it sinks slightly into the surface and stays in place, giving each biscuit its characteristic appearance.

items.prepNote: 1 for the dough, 1 beaten for egg wash

content.text: Combine {{plain-flour}}, {{almond-flour}}, {{caster-sugar}}, {{baking-powder}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}} in a large bowl. Rub in {{unsalted-butter}} with your fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse sand. Add 1 beaten {{eggs}} and {{vanilla-extract}} and mix until the dough just comes together. Press it into a ball; it should hold without crumbling. If it feels dry, add half a teaspoon of water. Wrap and refrigerate for 30 minutes.

Heat the oven to 175°C (conventional). Line two baking trays. Pinch off pieces of dough and roll into balls about 3 cm in diameter (roughly 20 g each). Place on the lined trays, spacing 3 cm apart. Press each ball down gently with the palm of your hand to about 1 cm thickness. Press one blanched {{almonds}} firmly into the centre of each round. Brush lightly with the remaining beaten egg.

Bake for 14 to 16 minutes until pale golden at the edges and the almond is lightly toasted. The cookies will feel slightly soft in the centre when pressed; they firm up as they cool. Leave on the tray for 10 minutes before transferring to a wire rack. They will be delicate while warm.
